newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow cardiology meeting mulls Yeltsin health.
newsitem.headline: Moscow cardiology meeting mulls Yeltsin health.

text.p: Cardiologists attending an international conference on Moscow on Tuesday have the world's most famous heart patient on their doorstep, but are still in the dark about what is wrong with him.

German heart surgeon Hans Borst, a speaker at the long-planned Moscow conference, said he thought the experts would happily advise Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who is in hospital with serious heart trouble.

"Logically the Russians should use the expertise presented by a group of at least 12 foreigners who are very well versed in this type of surgery," he said. "All of us are rather curious about what is going to be the next step."
Yeltsin, 65, breaking a long tradition of secrecy about the health of top Kremlin leaders, said on September 5 he was ready to undergo bypass surgery to resolve long-standing heart condition.
But his doctors have since expressed concern about whether he was fit enough for surgery.
Senior doctor Renat Akchurin, expected to lead the team of surgeons, said the operation might have to be postponed for up to eight weeks.

Participants at the conference, entitled blandly "The history of cardio-vascular surgery", include pioneering U.S. surgeon Michael DeBakey, who has already said he will join the team of doctors advising Yeltsin.
Interfax news agency quoted him as saying the doctors' meeting would take place on Wednesday.

DeBakey, who works in Houston and is 23 years older than his new patient, conducted the world's first successful heart bypass operation. "I'm always optimistic," he said when he arrived in Moscow on Monday.
Borst said DeBakey appeared to be the only doctor at the conference who had formally been invited to join the team of consultants to Yeltsin.

Possible help from Western advisers could include specialised post-operative care, especially if there were complications after surgery, Borst said. These could include pneumonia, lung infections and liver of kidney problems.

"The fact that he still has angina pectoris, heart pain on exercise, makes him a candidate to be operated on...but since the question is raised whether he should be operated on at all I wonder whether there are other snags which we do not know about yet," he added.

Asked if Yeltsin could stay president without an operation, Borst said: "If he has angina pectoris and it cannot be handled by drugs he cannot (stay in office), because he will drop out at the times he is most needed."
Russian communists, arguing that the president would not be able to carry out his duties fully if doctors did not operate, have said Yeltsin might have to step down.
"The situation in Russia is such that (the president) cannot have an easy work schedule," parliament speaker Gennady Seleznyov told reporters on Monday.
The medical conference has turned into a media circus where reporters and television crews almost outnumber doctors.
DeBakey and Russian cardiologist Leo Bokeria were due to hold a news conference at 5.30 p.m. (1330 GMT).
